scene.testo: Imagine you are floating outside a space station, 250 miles above Earth, moving at 17,500 mph. There is no floor. No wall. Just a thin tether between you and the void. This is a spacewalk, and astronauts say it is the most dangerous job in orbit.

Here is the question. Why would a person trained for years, who has flown rockets and lived in orbit for months, still feel fear at the airlock door? The answer is not one single danger. It is a whole list of them.

And the real danger is not what you would guess. It is not falling. In orbit, you cannot fall away. The real threats are quieter, and some of them have nearly killed astronauts in documented incidents. Stay with me, because it gets stranger.

Start with the suit. A spacewalk suit is not clothing. It is a tiny spacecraft shaped like a person. NASA's version is called the Extravehicular Mobility Unit, and it weighs about 300 pounds on Earth, roughly the weight of a grand piano's heavy leg.

Inside that suit, you carry your own air, your own water, your own cooling system, and your own radio. Nothing outside will keep you alive. No air to breathe, no pressure to hold your body together, and no way to cool down.

Now the temperatures. In direct sunlight in low Earth orbit, surfaces can heat up to about 250°F. Step into Earth's shadow, and they can drop to about minus 250°F. The station circles Earth every 90 minutes, so you swing between both extremes constantly.

Think about that. Your gloved hand might touch metal baking in sunlight, while your other hand grips a rail in freezing shadow. The suit has layers of insulation, but astronauts have reported cold fingers during long spacewalks, a documented problem.

Before you even leave, there is a problem called the bends. Your suit is pressurized at only about 4.3 pounds per square inch, far lower than the station's air. Nitrogen in your blood could form bubbles, just like a diver rising too fast.

To prevent that, astronauts breathe pure oxygen for hours before a spacewalk. This is called pre-breathing. It flushes nitrogen out of the body. It is boring, it is slow, and it is one of the most important safety steps in the whole process.

Then the hatch opens. The airlock air is pumped away until pressure drops to zero. Your suit puffs up and gets stiff. Every move now means pushing against the suit itself. Bending a finger becomes a workout, and it lasts for hours.

Spacewalks are long. Many last around six and a half hours. That is a full workday in a suit, with no bathroom. Astronauts wear an absorbent garment for that reason. Not glamorous, but it is the documented reality of the job.

And you are not alone out there with just a tether. NASA spacewalkers wear a backpack with a small jet system called SAFER. If a tether fails and you drift away, you can fire tiny nitrogen jets to fly back toward the station.

Why is that so important? Because in space, a gentle push never stops. No air to slow you down. If you drift away at a walking pace, you keep drifting. That is the fear almost every spacewalker mentions, simply floating away from the ship.

Now imagine the view. Earth glides past below you at 17,500 mph. Sunrise and sunset come every 45 minutes. Some astronauts describe it as the most beautiful sight of their lives. Others admit it can trigger a deep sense of vertigo.

There is no ground below you, only 250 miles of nothing. The brain struggles with that. Astronauts train for it, but even veterans have spoken about the strange feeling of hanging over the planet with only a thin suit as protection.

Next danger: the sun. Without the atmosphere, sunlight hits hard. Visors have special gold coatings to protect your eyes. Without that coating, the glare would be dangerous. The suit also has outer layers made to resist ultraviolet light.

Then comes something invisible: radiation. Outside the station's walls, you have less shielding. Most of the time, low Earth orbit is still protected by Earth's magnetic field, but during solar storms, NASA can delay or cancel spacewalks for safety.

And then there is the thing nobody can fully control: space junk. Tiny fragments of old rockets and satellites orbit Earth at incredible speed. A paint fleck moving that fast can crack a window. The station has actually been hit before, and NASA has documented it.

Meteoroids add to the risk. Small natural particles zip through orbit too. The suit has multiple layers designed to resist tiny impacts, but no suit can promise perfect protection. Engineers call it a managed risk, not a zero risk.

Mission control watches this closely. Teams track debris and plan around it. If a large piece is expected to pass close, the station can even fire thrusters to move out of the way. This is called a debris avoidance maneuver, and it is real.

But the scariest story of all is about water. July 16, 2013. Italian astronaut Luca Parmitano was on a spacewalk outside the International Space Station when he noticed water floating inside his helmet. It was documented by NASA and by Parmitano himself.

At first, it was a small amount. Then it grew. Water gathered around his head, covered his eyes, and flowed toward his nose. In zero gravity, water does not fall. It clings to your face. And it kept coming.

Parmitano later described that he could not see, could barely hear, and was worried about breathing. The danger was real. Water in a helmet can block your air and cause drowning, even in space, hundreds of miles from the nearest hospital.

Mission control called the spacewalk off. Parmitano had to find his way back to the airlock almost blind, guided by his memory of the station and by his partner's help. He followed the safety handrails back toward the hatch.

He made it inside. The crew quickly closed the hatch, repressurized the airlock, and removed his helmet. Investigators later found the leak came from a blockage in the suit's cooling system, and NASA changed procedures to prevent a repeat.

Afterward, NASA added a small snorkel-like tube and absorbent pads inside the helmets as extra safety. That is how spaceflight works. Every close call becomes a new rule, a new tool, a new line in the checklist.

Now step back in time. March 18, 1965. Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in history, floating outside Voskhod 2 for about 12 minutes. But the trip nearly ended in disaster, and the story is documented in his own accounts.

In the vacuum, his suit ballooned. It stiffened so much that he could not bend his hands to reach his camera. Worse, he could not fit back into the airlock. His suit was too swollen to squeeze through the opening.

Leonov made a bold choice. He opened a valve and let some air out of his suit, lowering the pressure. That made the suit smaller, and he managed to wriggle in headfirst. It was a risky move, because lowering pressure can cause the bends.

He survived. And that story shows why spacewalks scare astronauts. Even simple tasks, like going back through a door, can turn into life and death problems when you are wearing a suit that is also your life support.

Fast forward to the shuttle era. Astronauts used spacewalks to repair the Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990. Hubble flew about 340 miles above Earth, higher than the station, which made those repair missions even more demanding.

On those missions, astronauts worked on delicate equipment in bulky gloves. Imagine replacing a camera or tightening a bolt while wearing thick mittens, floating in a suit, with every tool tethered so nothing drifts away forever.

Tools are a real worry. A dropped wrench does not fall. It floats away and becomes a tiny satellite. That is why every tool has a tether, and why astronauts practice for years in a giant pool before ever going outside.

That pool is the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston. It is about 202 feet long, 102 feet wide, and 40 feet deep, holding roughly 6 million gallons of water. Inside, there is a full-size model of the station.

Astronauts spend many hours in that pool for each hour they will spend outside. Divers float beside them for safety. Water mimics weightlessness well, but it is not perfect, so the real thing always feels different.

Fatigue is another danger. Spacewalks demand constant focus. Your hands squeeze the gloves with every movement, and forearms burn. Astronauts have described sore fingers and even lost fingernails after long sessions, a documented effect of glove pressure.

Then there is the oxygen clock. Your suit carries a limited supply. If something goes wrong, you do not have hours to spare. Every spacewalk is planned minute by minute, with consumables tracked by teams on the ground and by the astronaut.

Compare that to a normal workday on Earth. A construction worker on a tall building can stop, take off a helmet, and drink water. A spacewalker cannot stop, cannot remove anything, and cannot step outside the suit for hours.

Picture the Empire State Building, about 1,454 feet tall to its tip. A spacewalker works at an altitude about 900 times higher than that. And unlike a skyscraper worker, there is no ground below to catch a mistake.

The pressure of that responsibility is heavy. One wrong move could damage the station, or the suit. Yet astronauts also say the work is deeply satisfying. Fixing a pump or a power unit outside keeps the whole orbiting laboratory alive.

Over the decades, astronauts have completed hundreds of spacewalks at the International Space Station. Each one follows the same rule: plan everything, rehearse everything, and keep the option to stop. Safety always beats the schedule.

Spacewalks also changed the world. Astronauts built the station piece by piece, installing solar arrays that stretch longer than a football field's width. Those arrays power the lab, and they were assembled by humans in suits.

So, why do astronauts fear spacewalks more than anything else? Because launch has abort systems, and the station has walls. Outside, you are alone with a suit, a tether, and a clock. Everything depends on equipment working perfectly for hours.

Yet here is the most surprising detail. Many astronauts say that after the fear passes, a spacewalk becomes the highlight of their career. They describe silence, brilliant light, and a view of Earth that no photograph can match.

Fear and wonder, in the same breath, 250 miles above your home. That is the paradox of the spacewalk. The most dangerous job in orbit is also the one astronauts remember forever. And the next crew is already training for it.

descrizione:
Why do astronauts fear spacewalks more than anything else? What really happens to astronauts when they float outside the space station, 250 miles above Earth, moving at 17,500 mph? The truth about spacewalks is stranger than you think.

From the helmet that filled with water in 2013 to the first spacewalk in 1965, we explore the real incidents, the suit, the radiation, the space junk, and the training that keeps astronauts alive. All facts come from NASA, ESA, and astronauts' own accounts.
